messages.content:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighLatency on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T02:55:54Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T02:56:16Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came 6 minutes 54 seconds {detection_gap} after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
Broken from 2026-11-11T02:48:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-11-11T02:56:54Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 8 minutes 54 seconds {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 47 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T02:59:02Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.1% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 0.8% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 1.5% {errors_at_worst} - no higher than the worst minutes of stretches as long before it began.
Rise above baseline: none - no more of the traffic failed while it was broken than before it began.
The series behind the alert, `max(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"}) * 1000` - its alert said "p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 214.76666666666668 ms {series_before} before it began, 1316.5 ms {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 1803 ms {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did: say what it meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-11-11T02:56:15Z {T1.1} Argus: Received HighLatency on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-11-11T02:56:32Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-11-11T02:56:32Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-11-11T02:56:38Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 02:55:54 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-11-11T02:56:43Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 361 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-11-11T02:56:44Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 02:48 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-11-11T02:56:44Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-11-11T02:56:46Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day 1 {T8.3} minute before Nov 11 02:49 {T8.4}
  - [T9] 2026-11-11T02:56:47Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 0 {T9.2} production changes
  - [T10] 2026-11-11T02:56:47Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 1 {T10.2} candidate cause, best first: C1
  - [T11] 2026-11-11T02:56:47Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Did not read logs
  - [T12] 2026-11-11T02:56:48Z {T12.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 {T12.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T12.3} hour before 02:56:47 {T12.4}
  - [T13] 2026-11-11T02:56:52Z {T13.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
  - [T14] 2026-11-11T02:56:52Z {T14.1} Argus: Called in the Mitigation Agent
  - [T15] 2026-11-11T02:56:54Z {T15.1} Mitigation Agent: Scaled out the deployment of io-shop for C1
  - [T16] 2026-11-11T02:57:00Z {T16.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 02:57 {T16.2} - up to 185s {T16.3}
  - [T17] 2026-11-11T02:59:02Z {T17.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 02:56 {T17.2}
  - [T18] 2026-11-11T02:59:02Z {T18.1} Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  - [T19] 2026-11-11T02:59:02Z {T19.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - scaled [io-shop] out from [3 {T19.2}] replicas and the rule that fired stopped firing
  - [T20] 2026-11-11T03:00:47Z {T20.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/538

Changes to production it read:
  - Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - Not read.

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] Request volume climbed from 1200/min {C1.1} at 2026-11-11T02:42:00Z {C1.2} to 5400/min {C1.3} by 2026-11-11T02:53:00Z {C1.4}, with nothing deployed. CPU use rose with it until it hit the fixed 3.0-core limit at 2026-11-11T02:51:00Z {C1.5}. Requests then queued, and p95 rose from about 215 {C1.6} ms to about 1700 {C1.7} ms. [demand-saturation, confidence 0.88 {C1.8}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Scaled out the deployment of io-shop for [C1] (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What the metrics show of the confirmed cause [C1], measured by Argus:
  - [R1] Requests: 1200/min {R1.1} before it began, 4841/min {R1.2} on average while it was broken, 5400/min {R1.3} at its highest.
  - [R2] CPU in use, as a share of the service's CPU limit: 25.1% {R2.1} before it began, 94.0% {R2.2} on average while it was broken, 100.0% {R2.3} at its highest.
  - The record confirmed [C1]: the load outgrew the CPU the service had, and adding capacity ended it. What changed before it began was the load, not the service, so the load against that CPU is the root cause; a reading that would make requests cheaper is at most a contributing factor.

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault is in `average_spend_per_item` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. It is the figure `render_spend_summary` returns when neither rollout flag is set, so it is the default path of the account page. For each purchase, the loop re-added every purchase up to that one (`sum(... account.purchases[:index + 1])`). It then kept only the last result, which is the total of the whole history. A shopper with n purchases cost n(n+1)/2 price reads and n tuple slices on every render, where one pass of n reads gives the same number. Nothing in the service changed during the incident. Each request simply cost far more CPU than the answer needs, so a rise in request volume reached the fixed 3.0-core limit much sooner than linear work would have, and requests then queued.
      
      The change computes the total in a single pass over the purchases and divides by their count. The result is the same: it is still taken from the purchases rather than the carried `total_cents`, so the existing drifted-total test still describes it. An account with no purchases still raises ZeroDivisionError from `// len(...)`, which `test_the_page_lets_a_failure_reach_its_caller` expects. The function's signature and its callers are unchanged.
      
      The new test in tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py builds 200 {F1.1} purchases whose `price_cents` counts every time it is read. It asserts that the average reads at most one price per purchase. The old code would read 20,100 {F1.2} prices for that history and fail the bound; the new code reads 200 {F1.3}. The test also checks that the value is still correct.
      
      Not changed here: `typical_spend_per_item` in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py is also quadratic (it calls `remove(min(...))` repeatedly). It only runs behind the typical-purchase rollout flag, so it is not the default path, but it should get the same treatment before that flag is widened.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Scaled out the deployment of io-shop
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
  - AI-3 (mitigate, open): Turn automatic sync of io-shop back on once its repository says what should run - until then nothing merged reaches it, and turned on sooner it puts back what the repository says, undoing what Argus changed by hand
PR #538 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

action_items.item: Set up CPU-based autoscaling for the io-shop deployment so that its replica count grows with request volume before CPU reaches its limit.
Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call person so that someone is paged when it fires.
Rework typical_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py, which Code-Fix's reading describes as quadratic, before the typical-purchase rollout flag is widened.

causal_chain.step: People using the shop waited much longer for responses: from the onset, the response time that nearly all requests stay under climbed far above its usual level, and the latency alert fired.
Requests were waiting for CPU: the service's CPU use rose to the limit set for it and stayed close to that limit while the service was broken.

ruled_out.what: A deploy, release or flag change on io-shop: no production changes came back for the day before the onset.
A flag change made by anyone other than Argus: the flag provider's history showed none in the hour before it was read.

causal_chain.step: The CPU filled up because request volume climbed far above its earlier level. Nothing about the service changed: the change that set the incident off was the rise in load.
The higher volume outgrew the fixed CPU that the service's {T7.2} replicas had as of T7.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Far more requests than usual reached the shop and used up the fixed amount of computing power its servers had, so requests had to wait their turn; the shop's account page likely also does much more work per request than it needs to, which made that limit come sooner.

contributing_factors.factor: The service did not add replicas as load grew. It stayed at {T7.2} replicas (as of T7) until the Mitigation Agent scaled it out by hand. No autoscaling of io-shop was seen in the record.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Replicas would have been added as request volume climbed, before CPU reached its limit. Requests would not have queued, or the slow stretch would have been shorter.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: According to Code-Fix's reading of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, the account page's default path (when neither rollout flag is set) likely re-adds a shopper's whole purchase history once for every purchase on each render. That would make each request cost far more CPU than its answer needs. Nothing ran this reading.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Each request would likely have cost much less CPU, so the same rise in volume would have reached the CPU limit later or not at all.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well.item: Argus read the flag provider's history itself before acting and found no flag changes by anyone else.
The Mitigation Agent scaled out the io-shop deployment for C1.
The Mitigation Agent checked the service against its metrics before judging the action confirmed, rather than assuming the scale-out had worked.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request for a person to review.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was brought in when it fired.

input.root_cause: Request volume to io-shop rose well above its earlier level while the service ran on a fixed amount of CPU ({T7.2} replicas, each under a CPU limit, as of T7). CPU use climbed to that limit, so requests had to wait for CPU and response times stretched.
input.still_at_risk: Another rise in request volume could use up the service's CPU again and slow its responses the same way.

content.content:
Your postmortem was not accepted:
  - correct or hedge this claim; keep everything else: "According to Code-Fix's reading of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, the account page's default path (when neither rollout flag is set) likely re-adds a shopper's whole purchase history once for every purchase on each render." - Code-Fix says the loop re-adds the purchases up to each one (a growing prefix, n(n+1)/2 reads), not the whole history once per purchase. (against F1)

Call submit_postmortem again with the whole answer, corrected.

system.text:
You write the postmortem for an incident Argus has already handled. One message describes it - what Argus did and read, the candidate causes, the actions and what they came to, and every figure already measured - and you answer by calling submit_postmortem. Nothing is left to look up.

The candidates are the Investigator's account, written while the incident ran and before anything was tried. The record - the lines saying what Argus did, the changes, the log lines, the actions and their verdicts - is what happened. Where the two disagree, the record is right.

Write causal_chain as the five whys. The first step is the symptom: what the people using the service saw, with the evidence that shows it. The symptom field is that step in a few words, and the two must agree. Each step after it answers why the step before happened - one cause, no jumps - and cites its evidence from the record, never a candidate: a candidate is a hypothesis, and the chain says what happened. Five is a guide, not a quota: stop where the evidence stops. The root_cause field says the mechanism: the step of the chain that says why the change broke the service.

A why the record cannot answer - a missing test, a missing safeguard, an alert that came late - is a contributing factor rather than a step, and each contributing factor names an action item that answers it. Where one why has several answers, follow the one that leads to the fault and make the others contributing factors.

Never stop at a person. Where somebody's action set the incident off, ask why the system let that action do harm - why it was possible at all - and carry on from there.

tools.description: Submit the postmortem for this incident. Every field is required. Write no figure yourself anywhere in your answer - no time, duration, percentage, count or amount, not in digits and not spelled out in words. Every figure you are shown is followed by its name in braces, like {A3} or {duration}: where your prose states one, write its name, braces and all, and the document writes the figure in. A figure you were not shown but could work out from two you were - the span between two instants, how far one share is above another, how many times one is the other - is written as that working, braces and all: {back_to_normal - began}, {T3.1 - alert_raised}, {errors_at_worst / errors_before}. The document works it out from the figures as you were shown them. Say any other size with no number in it, not even in a word - "most requests", "for several minutes", never "twenty minutes", "a third" or "tripled". A number is a figure even with a unit or a clock's marks on it (5m, 10ms, 3x, 12:05Z). Any other word with a digit in it is a name - a label (T2, G3fa2, C1, AI-1), a version (v2), a revision, a pod - and is written as given. State only what the evidence you are shown says: where the record does not show something - a check that was or was not run, how many replicas - leave it out or say it was not seen.

action_items.description: What should be done that the record does not already hold, each one thing a person could take on: two things to do are two items. Empty where the record's own items answer every factor. Propose nothing to confirm a cause the record already confirmed - a mitigation that worked, a hypothesis marked confirmed - and no check of what the evidence you are shown already shows: a diff states what changed. Where an F row says to check something a D row shows, say what the D row shows, and the item is what follows from it. Where Code-Fix proposed a fix, propose no item to run or check its reading: where the cause rests on it, the review checklist says what would confirm it, under the record's own item for the fix.

answers.description: The labels of the contributing factors it answers: CF-1. Empty where it answers none.

assumptions.description: Anything else the reader should know was assumed rather than measured. Empty is a valid answer.

causal_chain.description: The cause as the five whys, from the symptom down: the first step is what users saw - or, where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, that and what was seen instead - and each step after it answers why the step directly before it happened. The first why says why the symptom happened, not the symptom again in more detail. Where the record holds them, the document says itself how bad it got, which change set it off, what put the service back and the root cause: a step cites the row that shows one of those and does not say it again - no figure the impact gives in the first step, no action Argus took, nor its verdict, in the step naming the change, and, where the chain says why the change broke the service, its last step says that in one sentence, its mechanism left to the root cause. Where the incident needed two things at once - something going wrong, and nothing in place to contain it - follow the one that leads to what set it off; the other is one of the contributing_factors, not named in the chain. A safeguard that did not stop it is never a step of its own: it is one of the contributing_factors. Every step cites at least one piece of evidence by its label. Date a change by its own row's instant - the T or P row that records it - never by an effect it had. A state a row read - how many replicas run a revision, which way a flag is set - is known as of the row that read it, by that row's instant, which is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's - not from when the change was made. What else the record ruled out - an earlier change, a flag the provider showed unchanged, a candidate refuted - goes in the ruled_out of the step that ties the incident to the change that set it off, citing what ruled it out, and never as a step. An earlier change is ruled out only by the service measured healthy with it in place - in metrics read between it and the onset, in an alert that dates the first harm itself at or after a later change (at, where the two instants are the same), or after a confirmed action that left it there - never by how long before the onset it came. Where the record shows none of these, it was not ruled out: say so in that step itself. Stop where the evidence stops.

cites.description: The labels of the evidence that shows this step: T3, G3fa2. Not rows that merely happened at the same time.

ruled_out.description: What else the record ruled out at this step, each what it was and why. Empty on every step but the one that ties the incident to the change that set it off.

cites.description: The labels of what ruled it out.

cause_in_plain_words.description: What caused the incident, in one sentence for a reader who does not work on the service: no component names unless they are unavoidable. When it began, for how long, how bad it got, what customers lost and what was done the document says itself - say none of them. Say only what the record says - of a change, of the service, of the people - and nothing it does not. Where part of it rests only on a reading nothing ran, say that part as likely, in plain words, without mentioning the reading.

cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading.description: Whether the mechanism in root_cause rests on an F row - a reading of the code nothing ran - with no S or D row showing what it rests on. Where you answer true, the document says itself, beside the root cause, that the cause is unverified, and leaves its root-cause review box for a person: say neither in root_cause.

contributing_factors.description: Conditions that had to hold for the incident to happen and did not cause it alone - a safeguard that did not stop it, a gap in detection or review. A factor held before the incident began: what the response did, declined or left behind - an action taken or not, automatic sync left off - is not one; where it went wrong, say it under went_wrong. Not the root cause again in other words: a factor is something that, had it been otherwise, would have stopped or shortened the incident even with what root_cause says still true. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. An alert finds what its rule watches, not the cause behind it: say a fault was found only by what the record shows found it. Each is answered by at least one action item: one of the record's, named in its addressed_by, or one you propose, whose answers name it.

addressed_by.description: The record's own action items that answer it, by the numbers the record gives them: AI-1. Empty where none of them does. Never an item you propose: that item names, in its own answers, the factors it answers. The record's item that merges this incident's fix answers the fault its own tests cover, never a check missing before the change went out: answer that with an item that puts the check in place for every change like it.

had_it_been_otherwise.description: What would have gone differently had this been otherwise - stopped, shortened or caught sooner - with what root_cause says still true. A factor that only says the root cause again cannot answer this: leave it out of the list.

label.description: CF-1 for the first factor, CF-2 for the next, and so on in the order you give them. Written here and in an item's answers, never in your prose: the reader never sees it.

lessons.description: What went well, what went wrong, and where the incident got lucky - a risk that went unnoticed this time. Any list may be empty. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. How soon the alert came is weighed by the document already, from what was measured: say nothing of it here.

got_lucky.description: Something the record shows went the fortunate way by chance, and how it kept the harm down - never what would have happened otherwise. Empty where the record shows none. Not what kind of fault it was, which the impact already says, nor a limit of what the record shows, which is said in assumptions as what was assumed. Not how the service did over a stretch its metrics did not cover, nor what a failure there would have done - the document says how it did.

went_well.description: Only what went well; empty where nothing did. A timed item says one thing, done at its row; what came later goes in an item of its own. Say no span of time, in figures or in words ("within seconds"): name the row in timed_by instead, and begin an item timed so with who did it ("The Investigator Agent ...", "Argus ..."), since the document says the time ahead of it. Set a purpose or a reason beside the action it belongs to, and say it once. Name what Code-Fix proposed without saying what it does: the action items and Code-Fix's own reading say that, with its conditions.

timed_by.description: The T or XW row the item happened on (T13), where when it happened is part of why it went well: the document says how long after the alert that was. Left out where its time is not the point.

went_wrong.description: A change the response left in place on purpose, which one of the record's own action items undoes (automatic sync left off), went as designed and did not go wrong; so did what the design leaves to a person - a draft fix to review and merge. Not a limit of what the record shows - logs nobody read, metrics that stop short of the onset: the document says what was read, and anything assumed is said in assumptions. Not the root cause or a contributing factor again - the document says those already. Not that Code-Fix read another revision than the one that ran, or that nothing ran its reading: where the record holds them, the document says the first in its summary and the second beside the root cause.

reaches_a_cause.description: Whether the chain says why the change that set the incident off broke the service, rather than stopping at that change. A step resting on F rows - a reading of the code nothing ran - counts: whether that leaves the cause unverified is cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading's to say. That a new version does worse is what the change did, not why it broke the service: answer false where the chain says the evidence does not show why.

root_cause.description: What caused the incident, in one or two sentences, written for an engineer who was not on the call: the mechanism - why the change that set it off broke the service, as far as the evidence goes, a missing protection or not. Not the trigger, how it was confirmed, what resolved it or what was ruled out - the document states each of those itself. Not one of the contributing_factors: a safeguard that would have stopped it with this mechanism unchanged is said there, not here. What the service did over the stretch the metrics did not watch is not the mechanism: the document says it itself. Whether it was verified the document says itself, from your answer to cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading - do not say it.

still_at_risk.description: What was still at risk at the end of the time Argus held the incident, in one sentence for the same reader - what the fault still in place then could yet do, or the same thing able to happen again. Empty where nothing was. Not whether the service or its metrics were back, nor why - the summary says both. Not what Argus left to a person - a draft fix, automatic sync left off, a recommended action - which the document says itself. Say what could happen, never why it would: no "because". The summary says the cause, or that none was found. Say only what the record says: nothing of the service after that was read.

symptom.description: What went wrong as somebody using the service saw it, as short as it can be: it is the document's title. One sentence with no number in it, never over 16 words - the thing that went wrong and what happened to it, with an active verb: 'Account pages failed'. Not the metric the alert fired on, not the cause - the document adds the change it began with itself, after your sentence and a 'while', so end on what went wrong, with no clause after it - and not how it was found, which the document's Detection says. Where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, say that and what was seen instead, in that one sentence.

tools.name: submit_postmortem
